Name: Steven Haddock
Question: UiF the Big Bang happened with hydrogen and helium, what created those elements? And if you can answer that, what created their origin? Assuming the Big Bang theory is accurate, how did we end up with such precise detail?
Answer: No. The Big Bang didn’t star with “hydrogen and helium”. Hydrogen didn’t exist for 380,000 years after the Big Bang and helium didn’t come into existence in significant quantities until about 100 million years after that. In the first two minutes of the history of the universe, you had four things - photons, electrons, protons, and neutrons. Those are the building blocks of atoms, but they weren’t atoms yet. About three minutes in, you get hydrogen nuclei, but no hydrogen atoms. That’s because the early universe was incredibly hot and dense. 3 minutes in, it’s only about 60 million kilometers across, but still contains all the matter and energy that will ever exist in the universe. At those temperatures and pressures, atoms simply cannot form and stay together. Electrons and nuclei pretty much float around separately for hundreds of thousands of years until finally its cool enough for some electrons to become more or less permanently attached to a nuclei, forming the first hydrogen atoms. And even then, when we have hydrogen, it’s still too hot and dense for any bodies to be held together by gravity (which is a very weak force compared to the other fundamental forces) . After 100 million years, the universe is finally cool enough for some hydrogen to coalesce permanently under gravity and form a star. At that point, the star starts making helium. To make hydrogen, you need one electron and one proton - that’s it. You can add one or two neutrons, but you don’t really need them. However, only hydrogen atoms with one neutron can fuse to form helium, which has two protons and two neutrons. That’s the same process that powers our sun. And we’ve been able to work all this out using mathematics and looking for clues in astronomical observations, like “how far away are the furthest away galaxies”. You don’t see galaxies at the very limits of observation (only background radiation from the Big Bang) so you can date the formation of stars from the distance between the background radiation and the furthest away galaxies. The rest involves calculating the nature of the universe at every point and determining how much temperature and pressure would have to drop. We can reverse that process on earth (that’s what particle accelerators do) and see how much energy we have to put into a reaction to, for example, destroy atoms The answer is “not all that much and certainly a lot less energy than their was in the very early universe”.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: How does the "Big Bang" theory explain the movement of objects since the "big bang" event? Was there anything in existence before this event that could have caused this movement?
Answer: First and foremost, there was no “before” the Big Bang. Time, as we know it, started with the Big Bang and, due to relativistic effects of massive gravitational bodies, which the very early (e.g. first second) was, time got horribly dilated so from our standpoint that period of time from “zero seconds” to “one second” essentially took “forever”. In a nutshell, being in a very strong gravitational field (which still exist in black holes) is the same at travelling at “relativistic velocities” (i.e. very near the speed of light) so any person in a strong gravitational field or travelling near the speed of light would perceive time much more slowly than a person at more or less normal speeds and gravitational forces. You can think of it something like as much time passed between “zero seconds” and “one second” as has passed between “one second” and “now”. And, second, we have a name for the force that not only keeps the universe expanding but makes it expand faster with every passing second. It’s called “dark energy” and we’re just getting our heads around it, but given our observations of the universe there must be some sort of force that counteracts gravity to keep the universe from collapsing in on itself.

Question: For those who work in a law office: What is the craziest thing anyone wanted to sue someone about?
Answer: There was a rich businessman here in Toronto, a widower with three kids, all of whom he had already made arrangements to provide for so most of his estate was going to go to charity. He was getting on in years and found companionship with an older lady. Naturally, as people do when they get older, he became increasingly unable to handle his own affairs. However, he had thought ahead and had already created a committee of three other men, all titans of industry, to manage his affairs if that happened. So when it did, our rich man’s lady friend found that they were essentially putting her on a generous allowance rather than allowing her to buy whatever she wanted. So she came to us to go to court and install her as the rich man’s substitute decision maker. Now, please note that this would not have been a problem had they been married, and they were on the verge of doing so, but one of the rich man’s friends reminded him before the ceremony that if he did get married, his carefully laid out estate plan would be thrown into absolute chaos which would most likely attract massive tax consequences, so he backed out. Here’s the thing - we took on the case thinking we would get a big payout. There was a massive amount of money involved. But problems presented themselves immediately. First, if a person chooses a substitute decision maker, the court is unlikely to replace them unless they’re doing something self-serving. Like I said, these three guys were all of the highest reputation and they had all known the rich guy for decades. They were doing a first rate job and were working well together. However, our client had a series of old fraud convictions. Also, she stood to massively benefit if she was appointed. It took virtually no time for the court to reject our application entirely. Her previous fraud convictions were the nail in the proverbial coffin. The rich guy eventually passed and she worked out a settlement with the estate for ongoing support, which she was entitled to. The amount she received was about three times what I made in a year. And we never did get paid.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: How does QE differ from interest rate cuts?
Answer: You can only cut interest rates so low. How does 0% sound? Yeah, if you’re a central banker a lot of banks are going to take you up on that, but there’s no guarantee they will so anything but sit on the money, and in an economic crisis where there’s deflation and high unemployment that’s the last thing you want. Maybe you could loan banks money and have you pay less money back - negative interest. Same problem. So the deal with Quantitative Easing is that if a bank comes to you showing they loaned out money, you do lend them that money at zero interest. They make money from charging interest on the loan, and it meets the government’s policy of increasing the money supply without the risk that the money will just be sitting in a vault somewhere.

Question: Were any languages influential in the development of written Chinese characters?
Answer: No. Like Egyptian and even our own alphabet, Chinese characters were originally ideographs - visual representations of what they were supposed to represent. Over the roughly 3,000 years that Chinese has been a written language, the characters have become more stylized than representative, and the written language remained ideographic while Egyptian and Phoenician (and later Greek and Latin) became phonetic. As you can see, “horse” looked like a horse, “cart” looked like a cart and so on. However, about 2,300 years ago the hard to draw ideograms were morphed into slightly easier to draw abstract characters. Similarly, in the middle east, Egyptian started as a completely ideographic language, then sounds were assigned to some of the ideographs. For example, the /i/ sound was represented by an ibis, a very common bird in Egypt. Phoenician script was originally based on representing trade transactions that were often put on clay tablets, then they too started using the symbols to represent sounds. For example, “Aleph”, meaning “Ox” came to represent the /a/ sound. If you turn the Phoenician character 90 degrees counterclockwise, you can see the head and horn of an ox. The Chinese never switched to a phonetic alphabet because the ideographic characters work for all spoken forms of Chinese, which are otherwise unintelligible. Take this warning label Seven of the warnings are in the Roman alphabet, but they all have to be different because the languages are different. However, there’s only one Chinese warning that can be understood by anyone who can read Chinese writing, whether they speak Mandarin, Cantonese or Hakka. Japanese and Korean speakers were so impressed they adapted Chinese ideographs to represent sounds in their own language. The Japanese set, kanji, is still in common use but Korean has more recently abandoned that script in favour of Hangul, which is easier to learn.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Is Tim Hortons really Canada's favorite coffee and compared to what?
Answer: Tim Hortons is popular because for roughly the past twenty years they went on an aggressive expansion phase, ignoring conventional wisdom about how many people you needed to support a donut shop (the conventional wisdom - 4,000) . You see, in the early 1990s many people in smaller communities with pretty much no franchises were being ignored because the conventional wisdom was “that community can’t support a donut shop”. This is Meaford, a community of about 4,000 in Ontario on Georgian Bay. Ignore the franchises for the moment. I am familiar with the town because my uncle lived here in the 1970s and 1980s and really the only thing they had was a KFC and that was pretty much only a takeout location. As you can see now, it has a McDonalds and a Dairy Queen, but they’re both pretty new. Anyway, some enterprising entrepreneurs decided to have a go of it with donut shops in communities of about 1,000 people or so. The donut chains predicted failure. They thrived. Anyway, back in the 1990s, Tim Hortons had a partnership agreement with Wendy’s where they would build co-locations. There are still a lot of them around. The theory was that Wendy’s would benefit from the lunch and dinner hours and Tim’s from other times while they shared the same space. When the data on small town donut shops started to come in, Tim’s realized it had made a mistake and it really hurt the partnership as Tim’s went on a massive expansion spree that Wendy’s thought was a total mistake. It wasn’t. Tim’s thrived while Wendy’s faltered in Canada. So, anyway, here are the Tim’s near where I work Here are the ones near where I live Here are the ones near where I grew up And the ones near where my sister lives And the ones near where I stay when I go to Niagara Falls Lots of other Canadian consumer companies have taken the same route with the same success Dollarama A&W Popeye’s But, to be fair, there’s only one Tim’s in Meaford.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What are some notable NFL plays, both good and bad?
Answer: GOOD - The “Music City Miracle”. As much as it pains me as a Bills fan, this play was practiced and executed. The Bills had scored late to take a one point lead. However, there was only time for a kickoff as there wasn’t enough time on the clock to catch the kickoff and down the ball to get another play. However, the Titans had practiced a contingency play for just this situation all year, and when the Bills kicked off short, the ball receiver threw a lateral to a teammate near the sideline who had blocking in front of him and he ran for the winning touchdown. BAD - Rocket Screen - Super Bowl XVIII The heavily favoured Washington Redskins were down 7 points with 12 seconds left in the first half, but they were on their own twelve yard line. Coach Joe Gibbs remembered a play called “rocket screen” (a pass behind the line of scrimmage to the sideline) had gone for a long gain earlier that season. However, the team they had run that play against was the same team they were facing - the Oakland Raiders. The Raiders perfectly read the play and intercepted the pass for a pick-six putting them up by 14 going into the half. GOOD - Beastquake Leading by four points in the fourth quarter with about 3:40 left to play in the game from their own 32, the Seattle Seahawks were 2nd and 10 after no gain on the first play. The Seahawks, although playing at home, were underdogs as they won their division with a 7–9 record (to that point, the worst division winning record in history) and were playing the 11–3 Saints, who were just nosed out of first place in their own division. In an obvious passing situation, the Saints decided to play its linebackers wide leaving the center of the field open. The Seahawks attacked the center by handing the ball to Marshawn Lynch who used the lack of linebacker support to push through the initial tackling and find space, then accelerated quickly shedding tackles all the way for an amazing 67 yard touchdown run. BAD - The opening safety - Superbowl XLVIII In the comeback story of the year, the legendary Peyton Manning recovered from a neck injury to win the MVP award in 2014 and lead the Denver Broncos to the Super Bowl. However, on the first play from scrimmage, a miscommunication between Manning and his center resulted in the ball being snapped while Manning looked away and it was all Manning could do to rush back and cover up the ball to concede a safety. The Broncos never recovered and lost 43–8. GOOD - Plexico Burress’s go-ahead touchdown, Super Bowl XLII The 18–0 New England Patriots were heavy favorites over the 13–6 New York Giants, particularly due to the fact they had beat them in the final game of the regular season. However, late in the fourth quarter, the Patriots were ahead only 14–10 with the Giants pressing. However, on the previous play, Giants QB Eli Manning had shed a sack to throw a pass downfield to receiver David Tyree that Tyree caught on top of his helmet. That gave the Giants a first down on the Patriots fourteen with only 39 seconds left. It’s at that point that the Patriot’s defensive captain decided to go with an all-out blitz to try to force the the Giants back and perhaps end the game. However, Eli Manning spotted it and decided to target Plexico Burress who was facing single coverage. Burress ran deep into the endzone and caught a beautiful pass to put the Giants ahead. BAD - The Colt’s flea flicker, Super Bowl III The Colts were the heavy favourites against the New York Jets in the early NFL/AFL format of the first Super Bowls, the NFL had dominated. The Colts had only lost one game that year and had blown through the NFL championship while the Jets had struggled all year and eked out a win in the AFL championship. However, the Colts game plan wasn’t working against the speedy Jets defensive backs and late in the first half the Colts were trailing by more than a touchdown. In an attempt to kick start the team, they called a “flea flicker”, a fake run where the ball would be sent back to quarterback Earl Morrall who would throw it downfield for a big gain. Unfortunately, he missed a wide open receiver and tried to force it to another receiver and got intercepted. The Jets won the game 16–7.

Question: Are the Jews indigenous to Palestine, or was the latter just promised to the Jews in their sleep?
Answer: Except during the Babylonian exile (587 BCE to 539 BCE) where the Babylonians spent roughly a decade from 597 to 587 deporting Jews to Babylon, the area around Jerusalem has always been inhabited by Jews since the Exodus in roughly the 13th century BCE. Jews remained the majority of people in Palestine until the 4th century CE (so, for about a thousand years) until Christian pilgrims started to outnumber them in the 5th century. By the 12th century, the area was majority Muslim. The low point was in the late 17th century where there were probably no more than 2,000 Jews in the region compared to about 219,000 Muslims and 11,000 Christians, but even in 1800 their numbers had grown to about 7,000 although they still remained only about 3% of the population.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What movie is wonderfully awful?
Answer: FLASH! AH-AHH! “Flash Gordon” is not a well made movie. Its screenplay was written in English, translated into Italian for the Italian producer, and then re-translated back into English. The special effects are hokey (especially compared to “The Empire Strikes Back”, released the same year). The acting is sometimes just plain bad. The costume and set design are totally over the top. The star, yes the guy playing “Flash Gordon”, left before filming was completed over a contract dispute. But the movie is wonderfully entertaining from start to finish. If you’re willing to overlook its flaws, it’s story structure is solid, its pacing is great, its editing is amazing, and its use of a rock music soundtrack at key moments just works well. I saw it four times its opening weekend. It may not be something you want to show to film students (unless you want to point out its flaws) but people love it. It was Queen Elizabeth II’s favourite movie, and Charles III’s least favourite.

Question: Can the law regarding cell phone use while driving be changed in Ontario, Canada?
Answer: Of course it can. The current provision of the Highway Traffic Act was set by the legislature and can always be changed by the legislature. However, that’s unlikely. All studies point to cell phone use while driving being the equivalent of having a couple of shots of booze. In addition, statistics show that about 80% of accidents in Ontario are caused by distractions, and that includes cell phone use. The number of deaths from accidents in Ontario has doubled since 2000, and that matches the introduction of widespread adoption of cell phones and, later, smartphones.

Question: What are the differences between the Parliamentary System and American democracy? What is your opinion on the Parliamentary System?
Answer: The major difference is that in Westminster systems, such as the UK, Canada and Australia, the executive is part of and consistently has to answer to the legislature. In the American system, which is shared with other republics like France, the executive is completely separate from the legislature and does not need to answer to it on a constant basis, although there is a mechanism to remove the president. For example, in the UK, the Prime Minister actually has to be in the House of Commons twice a week while it is in session to answer questions posed by members of parliament. The U.S. president is under no obligation to answer to the legislature at any point. But the big difference is what happens at budget time. If the UK government proposes a budget (or indeed any provision to raise or spend money) and it doesn’t pass, Parliament can be dissolved and there can be another election or, at least, a change of Prime Minister. If the U.S. Congress can’t agree on a budget proposed by the president, the government just gets shut down and everyone keeps their job.

Question: Which movie star was the first to be born in Canada?
Answer: That would be this little lady right here Mary Pickford, born in Toronto in 1892. The site of her childhood home has a marker on University Avenue near what’s now Sick Children’s Hospital. And when I say “little” it’s because she was just a shade over 5 foot tall. Otherwise, she was a giant. After her Broadway play ended its run and she was out of work, she auditioned for D.W. Griffith, who was already a filmmaking legend by that point. She didn’t get the part, but Griffith realized that she had a handle on the difference between stage and film acting and offered her the immense sum of $10 a day (twice the going rate) and a guarantee of $40 a week. Mary made her film debut in the 1909 short “Mrs. Jones Entertains”, one of about fifty films she made that year. The following year, she moved from New York to Hollywood. Back in those days, actors didn’t get credits, but audiences soon noted Pickford and in her first year they clamoured to find out who she was. In 1912 she moved back to Broadway, but realized she preferred film acting and was soon back in Hollywood. By 1914, her name was appearing above the title on most of her features, and she was often demanding further raises. By 1916, she was making the unheard of sum of $10,000 a week, plus profit sharing. By the late 1910s, only Charlie Chaplin matched her in popularity. She was soon running her own film production company. When her contract expired in 1918, she left for more money, but by 1919 she, Chaplin and Douglas Fairbanks Sr. had enough money to start their own studio, United Artists. Her films were soon grossing over a million dollars each. Unfortunately, she mad a poor transition to talkies, and by the time she was in her thirties she could no longer play the young spirited characters that had made her such a success with audiences. Although she racked up an Academy Award, she largely retired from film acting in 1933 and focused on producing the movies of other people.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What is the breakdown of income tax distribution among the different levels of government in Canada?
Answer: Both the federal government and the provincial governments collect income tax, but under an agreement between them all the forms are federal, the federal government collects the money and then disburses it to the provinces. It varies by province but here in Ontario the provincial rate is roughly 25% of the federal rate across all income brackets, so 80% of the income tax you pay is kept by the federal government. For example, for the highest income earners, the top bracket is 53.53% of income for federal taxes, and 13.16% for Ontario taxes. Of course, municipalities get screwed because they don’t collect income tax. Almost all municipal revenue comes from property and commercial taxes collected locally, plus a few grants from the federal and provincial governments.

Question: Can an American citizen become a Canadian citizen through marriage? What is the process for doing so and what are the requirements, aside from marrying a Canadian?
Answer: No. Marrying a Canadian citizen will get you a fiance visa and, eventually, permanent resident status, but like any other immigrant you have to go through the waiting period to be eligible for citizenship (I believe it’s ten years at the moment), then pass the citizenship exam. You still have to apply for your fiance visa (whether you’re married or not) outside of Canada (it doesn’t have to be in the US, but that would be easiest). Once you’re married you can get permanent resident status and can reside in Canada, but you can’t get citizenship in Canada unless you continue to reside here (although you aren’t trapped in the country - you can still be out of Canada up to about 180 days in any given year as long as you have a permanent address in Canada). But please note that Canada has absolutely no respect for the institution of marriage, which means even if your marriage is 100% legit, legal and binding (Nevada anyone?) you can still be turned down if the immigration authorities don’t think the marriage is bona fides (i.e. is just a “marriage of convenience”). Cohabitation is the best way to prove that.

Question: Is it feasible for Israel to give up some of its territory to the Palestinians as a means of preventing attacks on its borders?
Answer: Back in 1993, as part of the Oslo Accords, both Israel and Palestine agreed the starting point of discussions about their respective territories would be the “Green Line” - the 1949 Cease Fire Line that constituted the de facto border of Israel until 1967. Now, Israel has controlled all former territory of the British Palestinian Mandate since 1967, but has never annexed any of it. None of that territory is recognized by Israel as “Israel”. That’s “Occupied Territory” or “Territory under the administration of the Palestinian Authority”. No other country recognizes any claim by Israel over any of that territory. Israel has said many times in many contexts that they are willing to cede this to the new Palestinian state. Nevertheless, about 700,000 Israeli citizens live on the other side of the Green Line. That includes Israelis living East Jerusalem, which many countries who recognize Palestine as a sovereign nation recognize as the capital of Palestine. That number just keeps growing every year. Although these “settlements” have no basis in Israeli law, they are actively supported by Israeli military forces in the area and are tacitly accepted by the Israeli government, which is doing nothing to stop the formation of new settlements and is not doing anything to get rid of the existing ones. This has not always been the case. In 1980 when Israel handed back the occupied Sinai to Egypt, it dismantled all the Israeli settlements in the area. In 1993 when Israel handed all of Gaza to the Palestinian Authority, it also dismantled all the Israeli settlements. Now, back in 1993, if Israel had simply handed pretty much all the territory over the Green Line to Palestine, Palestine would have accepted that. In 1993, the people in charge of the Palestinian authority were amenable to a settlement recognizing Israel’s claim to everything on their side of the Green Line. However, for practical purposes, which were recognized by the Palestinian Authority, the Palestinians realized that without Israeli help they could not control militants, so a phased handover was planned. That “phase” is now nearly a generation old and it’s gone nowhere. It’s not that the Israelis and Palestinians haven’t been talking. However, even moderate Palestinians objected to portions behind the Green Line remaining part of Israel. In addition to sovereignty issues, there are also land ownership issues - a lot of Israeli territory and settlements are on land owned by Palestinian Arabs who took title to the land before 1947 and haven’t actually had their land appropriated. Under Israeli law passed in 1950, if the Israelis find “abandoned” land, they can hold it in trust. It’s rented out to Israelis who don’t “own” it but are allowed to occupy it. There’s a lot of land in the West Bank that’s subject tot his law as well. It’s not that it wouldn’t be a good idea to adjust the actual border. However, the adjustments some Israeli negotiators want are over territory that’s very important to Palestine for a lot of reasons. It’s almost as if they pick land they know the Palestinians won’t give up. Complicating the fact is that Israel has built physical barriers that also go across the Green Line. Many of these actually cut off one Palestinian community from another. As such, for some Palestinians to go from “Palestine” to “Palestine”, the short way requires crossing two Israeli checkpoints. Going around the barrier usually requires going through even more Israeli military checkpoints. So what’s the solution? Why are you asking me. I haven’t got any idea. However, I am descended from people in Northern Ireland and I have relatives who lived there. One of the ways they solved the problem was taking down the border entirely. The only way you know now whether you’re in Ireland or Northern Ireland is that the maximum speed limit signs change from km/h to mph. Oh, and the pubs on one side take Euros and the other takes Pounds. The border was kept open even after the UK left the EU (Ireland is still in the EU).

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: When was the last Silent Movie released? When did sound completely take over in cinema?
Answer: The last silent movie was only released 13 years ago (this being 2024) “The Artist” was critically acclaimed and won five Oscar awards, including “Best Picture”. But it’s hardly the first such experiment. Mel Brooks went full comedy in “Silent Movie”, which unfortunately didn’t do terribly well critically or commercially. The film has only one piece of dialogue - famous mime Marcel Marceau being asked to be in the movie and replying “Non”. The last mainstream silent movie at the end of the silent era was Charles Chaplin’s “Modern Times” about a factory worker driven mad by his job who then has a series of adventures due to misunderstandings. By that time, silent movies were all but gone and this one was the first since 1931’s “City Lights”, also by Chaplin. But silent films pretty much died immediately once sound technology was introduced to film. “Wings”, which won the first Academy Award for “Best Picture” in 1929 was the last silent film to win that award until “The Artist”. In subsequent years, talking pictures dominated. In 1930, four of the five “Best Picture” nominees has synchronized sound and two, including the winner, were musicals. The fifth nominee, “The Patriot” had non-synchronized sound. As such the complete list of silent films nominated for best picture are “Wings” (1929), “The Artist” (2012) and “The Racket” (1929).

Question: Is there an animated movie that accurately portrays human history?
Answer: Well, not a movie, but there is an animated series Consisting of twenty-six twenty-five minute episodes, this animated series, made in France but financed widely by educational television providers all over the planet, covers all periods of human history using the same set of characters throughout. The first episode covers the history of earth from its formation in the solar system until the appearance of Homo Erectus. The last episode covers the period of time from 1945 to the production of the series in 1978, then speculates on the future. The characters (in English) are Maestro (the wise old man), Peter (the ordinary guy), Jumbo (the fighter), Pierette (the lady), The Pest (the villain), The Dwarf (The Pest’s boss), and The Clock (who visually provides the year events take place) Six other series in the “Once Upon a Time…” franchise have also been produced, each covering a less wide scope of time. Many of the episodes are available on YouTube

Question: How do umpires tell when a swing is checked?
Answer: To add to Mr. Murray’s answer, a swing is “full” if the top of the bat goes over the first base line for a right handed batter, or the third base line for a left handed batter. If the top of the bat doesn’t cross the line, it’s a “check swing” and it’s called either a ball or strike depending on whether the ball went through the strike zone. This rule prevents a batter from pretty much swinging with power from the handle alone without actually moving the top of the bat forward. A decent batter can actually chop the ball without having to move the top of the bat forward too much, but can’t accomplish that unless the top of the bat goes over the baseline. And it’s an appeal play. The home plate umpire can call “strike” without checking, but the batter can ask for a ruling from the base umpire, who can call either “strike” or “ball” based on their view of the swing.

Question: What are the options for using public transportation or taxis to navigate Montreal's underground city?
Answer: Montreal’s underground network, the RESO, is very spread out and some of the connections aren’t close to one another so it’s not easy to do the whole thing on foot. As is obvious, several Metro Stations serve the RESO, but there’s a problem - some are served by the Green line near Sherbrooke Ave., and some are served by the Orange Line near Boul. Rene Levesque. Those two streets aren’t terribly close together, and the two subway lines only meet at Berri-UQAM, which is at the far eastern end, and Lionel Groulx, which is off to the west. Navigating the RESO by car or bus is difficult because many of Montreal’s downtown streets are one-way and are interrupted by pedestrian plazas (like the one near Place des Arts all year, or the one in the Golden Square Mile during summer). Traffic also sucks, even if there’s no construction. Lastly, several clusters are ONLY connected by the Metro, not by pedestrian tunnels. Place Alexis Nihon is a good example. On the other hand, the heart of RESO with the most interesting destinations are all clustered around St. Catherine St. in the Golden Mile. I suggest you start there. Most of the best shopping is on the north side of St. Catherine between Peel and McGill where you will find The Bay, Simons and most of the other major retailers. Most of the rest of the system is just there for convenience. There’s also good shopping at Place Ville Marie south of St. Catherines, which also conveniently connects to Gare Centrale, the main intercity/commuter rail station.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: What is the appropriate term for the indigenous people of Canada, Inuits or Eskimos?
Answer: The indigenous people of the far north who aren’t culturally, genetically or linguistically related to any of the First Nations prefer “Inuit” which means “The People” in their language Inuktitut. “Inuit” is the proper plural. The problem with “Eskimo” is that it’s a borrowed term from Innu-aimun, an Algonquin language spoken by First Nations in Labrador. It’s original meaning is uncertain (probably “a person who laces snowshoes), but the Innu-aimun used it for both the Inuit and the Mi’kmac (another First Nation). the French adopted this term and it spread into English for all the people in the North from Greenland to Alaska.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Why would Pierre Poilievre's policy fail?
Answer: Well, Poilievre doesn’t have much in the way of policy. His strategy so far has been “Trudeau bad! Trudeau corrupt! Trudeau incompetent! Trudeau a laughing stock!” Now, there are people doing poorly in Canada, but that’s largely due to provincial policies, not federal ones. Trudeau is pretty much being blamed for things the federal government can’t do constitutionally. So let’s look at some of the barely enunciated policies shall we? Remover the carbon tax Or as he puts it “remove the inflationary carbon tax” which doesn’t hold up under scrutiny (the carbon tax accounts for only a small part of inflation). The problem is that the carbon tax, which I note that conservative premiers ganged up on to remove and LOST not because they said the federal government can’t impose it (which it clearly can) but because it wasn’t imposed on provinces that had their own carbon tax or cap-and-trade scheme, which two of those provinces already had and dropped, forcing a showdown. The problem is that Poilievre hasn’t told us what will replace it. Canada is one of the biggest per capita carbon dioxide producers (far more than the Scandinavian countries) and one of the problems with the carbon tax is that it’s generally far too low to dissuade people from using carbon based fuels. Yes we do need things like zero interest loans for alternatives (other energy solutions pay for themselves over time, even if there is no carbon tax) but the only reasonable alternative is “cap and trade”, which Ontario had until it dropped it to force a showdown. Quebec still has a cap and trade scheme it shares with California, and we’re already seeing transition (for example, maple syrup producers have switched from fuel oil driven evaporators to electric ones). Both the carbon tax and cap-and-trade were solutions that were developed by conservative leaning economists, and cap-and-trade worked brilliantly to reduce acid rain causing emissions. The left leaning solution would just be banning stuff that uses carbon based fuels. The other thing is that the vast majority of Canadians (85%) get more money from the government than they pay in carbon taxes. That’s because most carbon taxes are used by heavy industry (like the Alberta Oil Sands, which produces more carbon dioxide than all of Quebec). For example, Poilievre tried to use the example of an Ottawa region mushroom farmer whose carbon tax bill was about $100,000 a year, but that meant that the farmer was using more than $1 million of fuel a year in any event and it would probably make more sense to finance a heating system that was more energy efficient. Make housing more affordable The Conservative playbook on this has generally been “open up more greenspace to housing use” but even Ontario’s government, which tried and failed to do this, realizes that it’s not going to solve the problem because new housing on “greenfields” tends to be expensive single family homes and not affordable housing. But Poilievre can complain all he wants but the genesis of the affordable housing crisis was created by the Mulroney government in the 1980s, who followed the policy of the Reagan government and the Thatcher government - get the government out of the housing business and leave it to the market. However, “the market” wants housing prices to remain high to protect their investment. People in the UK who bought their council houses in the 1980s are sitting pretty right now, but they all know their children can no longer afford housing because of it. Now back in the 1970s, governments at all levels were building rent-geared-to-income housing and making money available for cooperative housing and other non-profit housing. I myself live in a 1970s cooperative and I pay about 60% of market for my unit. All that ended in the 1980s and attempts to build such housing since have been scattershot at best. And the big problem is not at the federal level, or even the provincial level - it’s at the municipal level where local zoning laws make it difficult or impossible to build affordable housing. Here in Toronto, local opposition can hold up approval of affordable units for years. One affordable development near by boyhood home, a beautiful location near a regional rail station, is permanently on hold because construction costs will make it unprofitable. Right now, it’s an empty lot. Lowering spending One of the really bad things that happened to the Conservatives last year is that the Liberals delivered a budget with a lower deficit, benefitting from the recovery of the economy after the high spending necessitated by the pandemic. Poilievre has said high deficits are bad, but delivered no alternative to the economic plunge in 2020 which the Trudeau government responded to by making applying for supplementary benefits far easier. That appears to have worked. But if you’re voting conservatives for “lower taxes”, please be assured that this just means “more debt”. Here in Ontario, the Progressive Conservatives got elected partly on the platform that the Liberals were spending too much money, forcing higher taxes. Since being elected, in every single year, Ontario government spending has gone up regardless of revenue projections, which were made worse by things like scrapping the annual vehicle plate registration fee (cost about $1 billion). That’s just meant higher deficits every year. Conservatives are not, and never have been, fiscally prudent. For example, Alberta’s budget still comes mostly from oil revenues, which just aren’t going to be sustainable, which is why they fight so hard against the carbon tax because it benefits provinces like Quebec which produce clean power (Quebec has been investing heavily in hydroelectricity since the 1960s, and it’s paid off big time).

Question: What is the basis of Israel's claim to land in Palestine? Is there a dispute over the amount of land it has taken over?
Answer: Okay, this is going to get complicated, but here we go. On May 15, 1948, the United Kingdom, gave up all of its claims to the Palestinian Mandate, having refused to even attempt to implement a plan by the United Nations from the previous November that would have split the territory into roughly seven different territories, some of which would be controlled by the provisional Jewish government of the territory, and the others that would be controlled by the local Arabs. Jerusalem would be administered by the United Nations. Here’s the plan, but don’t worry, it won’t be important later. Slightly prior to this, realizing there would be chaos once the British left, the Americans offered to continue a trusteeship of the territory until a suitable partition plan could be worked out, but they had no illusions that this would be pretty much impossible. The day before, on May 14, the Jewish provisional cabinet declared independence at a ceremony in Tel Aviv. This was almost immediately recognized by the United States and by the end of the week, the Soviet Union had also recognized the new government, now known as “Israel”. Israel had no fixed territory and both Jewish and Arab militias had been fighting each other since the end of World War II, with the Jewish militias also taking aim at the British authorities. As such, on May 15, 1948, the territory above belonged to no-one. The Arab-Israeli war, which lasted from May of 1948 to January of 1949, involved the new nation of Israel and a coalition of local Arab militias assisted by the armed forces of surrounding Arab nations. At first, the Arabs dominated the conflict, but by November an influx of Jewish volunteers and weaponry turned the tide, forcing the Arab forces back. In January of 1949 they agreed to a cease fire. All sides agreed the armistice line was not to be considered a “border”, and the Arab allies consistently refused to recognize any of Israel’s claim to any of the land it now occupied. However, Israel’s allies an very quickly after, the United Nations recognized the blue area as Israel’s territory. In the absence of any agreement to the contrary. With the Arab nations refusing to come to the table to discuss a peace treaty, this became the de facto border of Israel for the next 18 years. In the meantime, about 700,000 Arabs who had been living in the blue territory had been forced out, mostly into the West Bank. To make matters worse, Egypt and Jordan essentially asserted sovereignty over the areas that they occupied, but refused to recognize the Arabs living their as citizens. Part of that was that Palestinian Arabs refused to swear an oath of loyalty to the King of Jordan. In any event, the people who lived in Palestine didn’t identify as Egyptian or Jordanian, and the United Nations recognized them as “refugees” and still does. During this time, from a diplomatic standpoint, Jordan was the official representative of the Palestinian people as most Palestinian refugees lived in Jordan or the Jordanian West Bank. This proved to be untenable so in 1964 the Arab League formed the Palestinian National Council as the official representative of the Palestinian people. Unfortunately, Jordan and Egypt did not recognize the territory they occupied as “Palestine” and as such “Palestine” became only the territory that was controlled by Israel. It’s not like the Arabs didn’t try. In 1967, they planned a war to take back Israel. However, the “Six Day War” was an absolute disaster and not only left Israel in complete occupation of the Palestinian Mandate, but the Golan Heights of Syria and the Egyptian Sinai as well. However, Israel made no attempt to annex these territories, although some Israelis, with the tacit support of the government, set up what are now called “settlements” - areas controlled by Israeli citizens with the help of the Israeli military. Through this time, the Palestinian National Council, through their military arm the Palestine Liberation Organization, started a terrorism campaign against Israel in both the occupied territories and Israeli targets abroad (for example, the PLO staged a kidnapping and murder of Israeli athletes at the 1972 Summer Olympics in Munich). Another war in 1973 had no effect on the occupied territory, but it continued the shutdown of the Suez Canal (the Israeli’s occupied the west bank of the canal), but the 1973 was had been a close thing and by 1978 both the Israelis and Egyptians were willing to talk. This resulted in the Camp David accords where Egypt agreed to recognize Israel’s claim to its pre 1967 borders in return for the Sinai and cooperation against the PLO. But the terrorism continued and eventually the Israeli government, which had made it treason to talk to the PLO or the PNC, eventually planned a back door conference to be held between two Israeli representatives and a PLO representative under the cover of an academic conference in Oslo, Norway. The conference was successful and in return for a promise to return the occupied territories to the Arabs, the PLO recognized Israel’s claim to it’s pre-1967 borders, The Palestinian Authority was created as the territory’s provisional government and a framework was created to hand control to the PA from the Israeli military. Based on a promise that Israel would withdraw to its pre-1967 borders (the “Green Line”), Jordan dropped its claim to the West Bank and recognized Israel’s territory based on its pre-1967 border. However, there’s still no agreement 31 years later as Israel has built a wall which goes over the green line, and at present about 670,000 Israeli citizens live in the occupied territories, a number that grows every year. Israel did dismantle the settlements in the Sinai and in Gaza, but never the ones in the West Bank and East Jerusalem.

Question: What is the worst acting performance in a blockbuster that you have seen?
Answer: Oh, that has to be Dwayne Johnston in “Black Adam” Look. I get it. Johnson is a massive star and can bring box office success simply on the value of his name. Indeed, the film did very well overseas. But DC was betting heavily on this movie to drive the rest of the DC Cinematic Universe. It cost $195 million to make and only took in $168 million domestically. Like many DC films, it also failed to impress critics. Audiences liked it (it has an 88% on Rotten Tomatoes) but it’s clear that Johnson really doesn’t have what you would want to justify a sequel. By contrast, Zachary Levi, who essentially plays the mirror character, is a delight to watch on screen as he goes through a full range of emotions and makes us completely believe he’s a teenage boy in a mature man’s body. “Shazam” struggled at the box office too, but at least it justified a sequel and Levi played well off a good supporting cast. Johnson had a much better supporting cast in “Black Adam” but totally failed to connect with them. Both movies are deeply flawed but both “Shazam” movies have us feeling deeply for all the characters and when Billy sacrifices himself in “Shazam 2” it’s a deeply moving experience. No one cares if “Black Adam” makes it through the movie even though he undergoes a better redemption arc than Billy Batson did.

Question: Is it true that English is the language from which all the other languages of the world are descended? After all, isn’t English the language of God himself, because isn’t it the language of the Bible, as King James the First reputedly said?
Answer: That’s not even close to being true. “English” didn’t even exist as a separate language until about 600 C.E. That’s when we see the first texts written in the language and, at that time, the language looked like this: As far as we know, there is no “single root language”, but the oldest languages in the world are traced to the Bushmen, a group of people in southwest Africa who speak about 200 different languages that are mutually unintelligible And assuming that what we know about God is true, the first written texts about him are about two-thousand years older than the English language. And, as has been noted, the King James Bible wasn’t even the first English language bible. It was just the first royal approved translation as the King commissioned the translation and it became the standard for the Church of England thereafter. However, in previous centuries, all the Bibles in England most likely would have been in Latin because that was the language of the Catholic mass. Catholicism didn’t start doing mass in vernacular languages until the mid 20th century.

Question: Which major city does not have any interstate highways within its limits, such as New York City?
Answer: New York City has several interstates within its boundaries, including I-95 which passes right through northern Manhattan on its way to The Bronx But the six largest U.S. cities without an interstate in their boundaries are all in California - Fresno, Bakersfield, Modesto, Oxnard, Salinas and Santa Rosa. Name: Steven Haddock
Question: How many states are in the United States? Why do some countries have multiple states while others only have one?
Answer: The United States has forty-six states and four “commonwealths” (Virginia, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts and Kentucky) with the commonwealths being treated as states for all purposes. The United States is one of only a dozen or so countries that uses a “federal” system with sovereign sub-units within the main government, with a division of powers between the central government and the regional governments. Most states are “unitary” with only one central government that can pass laws of their own accord. Other countries that use a federal system are Canada, Australia, Switzerland, Germany, Brazil, Venezuela, Nigeria, India, Russia, Syria, Nepal, Pakistan, Argentina, Austria, Belgium, Bosnia & Herzegovina, Comoros, Ethiopia, Malaysia, Mexico, Micronesia, Saint Kitts & Nevis, South Africa, Spain and the United Arab Emirates. Yugoslavia also used to be a federal state, but it split up into individual countries in the 1990s.

Name: Steven Haddock
Question: Is it true that driving long distances on highways can make your car more fuel-efficient? If so, what is the reason behind this?
Answer: It’s actually the reverse - your car is more fuel efficient when it’s driving on a highway, assuming you don’t go overboard on the speed. “City Driving”, particularly in an internal combustion vehicle, is very fuel inefficient as you stop all the time (but still use fuel) and are constantly changing speeds. Your car is most fuel efficient when it is travelling at a constant speed. Fuel isn’t wasted when you speed up or slow down the engine to adjust to immediate conditions, or by stopping for traffic lights (although stopping for traffic isn’t good either). But there’s a catch - the faster you go the harder your engine has to work against mechanical and road friction to keep your speed up. There’s a “sweet spot” between about 55–65 mph where your car’s engine is the most comfortable and has the highest efficiency. Speeding up or slowing down wastes fuel either because your car isn’t working as efficiently (slow speeds) or you’re using too much fuel to overcome extra forces on your car (at high speeds).

Question: How does blood nourish and oxygenate organs in the body? Where does it come from and where does it go after leaving the capillaries in each organ?
Answer: Red blood cells originate in the bone marrow - the soft part inside the bones. They’re constantly being manufactured from raw materials that are usually created in the liver. Once created, they enter the bloodstream. Their sole job is to deliver oxygen to the body’s tissues. In lower forms of life, like bacteria, oxygen diffuses through the cell wall, or in insects it enters through cavities through the body. However, oxygen can only travel so far so this only works if your body tissues are all directly exposed to air or water. The main component of red blood cells that does the heavy lifting is a molecule called hemoglobin. Hemoglobin has a unique characteristic - where there’s lot of oxygen it likes to attach to oxygen molecules, but where there’s lots of carbon dioxide, it likes to attach to carbon dioxide molecules. It can freely exchange one for the other in those circumstances. So let’s start with a blood cell in the lower left ventricle of the heart. It’s pumped by the heart into the aorta, which is the largest artery (arteries carry blood from the heart, veins carry it to the heart). Some of that blood flow is diverted to the nearby coronary artery, which provides blood and oxygen to the heart muscle. From the aorta, red blood cells go down increasingly smaller arteries until they reach capillaries, which are just big enough for one red blood cell to squeeze through. Here, they’re pretty much in direct contact with cells which are constantly dumping carbon dioxide into the bloodstream as a waste product. At that point, since the concentration of carbon dioxide is so high, the red blood cell releases its oxygen molecule and takes up a carbon dioxide one. The oxygen molecule diffuses through the cell wall for use in metabolic processes. To this point, the blood has been under pressure from the heart (that’s “blood pressure”) but that’s lost in the capillaries so the return trip through veins takes advantage of a series of one way valves (arteries don’t need those) and muscle movement (which squeezes the veins and forces blood through them). The veins get larger and larger until you get to the inferior vena cava (from below) or the superior vena cava (from above), which leads into the upper right atrium of the heart. From there, it’s pumped into the lower right ventricle which forces it into the pulmonary artery, which leads to the lungs. Again, the arteries, now carrying de-oxygenated blood, get smaller and smaller until they reach pulmonary capillaries. These don’t run by living cells, but through the small air sacs of the lungs, which if you’re breathing properly should contain about 100 times more oxygen than carbon dioxide. With so much oxygen, the hemoglobin lets go of its carbon dioxide molecule and absorbs an oxygen molecule. The gases in the blood diffuse though the membrane of the air sac, and the amount of CO2 in the lungs increases - until you breathe out which gets rid of most of the CO2. Your feedback mechanisms will make you breathe harder if CO2 builds up in your lungs, and less hard if there’s lots of oxygen. From the lung capillaries, the pulmonary veins again start to converge into the pulmonary vein which enters your heart in the upper left atrium, which is pumped into the lower left ventricle and your blood cells are off again. Total time to make one lap - about one minute. Of course, red blood cells break down with use. The waste products eventually pass through the spleen and the liver where they’re recycled to make more raw materials for more red blood cells. The first guy to figure this out was a fellow named William Harvey, who drained a dead body of blood, then squeezed the heart to see how much blood it could pump. Knowing how fast the heart pumped (about 60–100 times a minute), he came up with the figure that all the blood could be pumped in one minute. The prevailing theory was that the heart made blood and the cells consumed it, but Harvey realized that it was impossible for the heart to create seven pints of blood in one minute. He did more dissection of dead bodies and discovered the answer - blood circulates. There are lots of diseases that effect red blood cell production. I had one - pernicious anemia. Vitamin B12 is a key component in blood production and if you don’t have any, your body can’t make enough blood. I wasn’t getting enough B12 in my diet (probably because I constantly microwave food - long story) so I started taking supplements and now I’m fine. Blood only provides nourishment by allowing nutrients, mostly sugar, to float around the body where it can be taken up by cells. Food is just along for the ride.

Question: How do scientists see evolution? Why do they brush off creationism as unscientific?
Answer: “Evolution”, a term coined by Charles Darwin’s grandfather Erasmus Darwin, started to come into the scientific consciousness as biologists started to look more deeply into vertebrate anatomy. The harder they looked the more they realized that the anatomy of every single vertebrate is pretty much a variation on the same set of bones. Even though all these vertebrates use their forelimbs for a different purpose, they pretty much have identical sets of bones. Some are smaller, some are larger, but they’re all connected to each other in the same way. Particularly striking is the similarities between bat wings and bird wings in function and basic bone structure, but not in the arrangement of those bones. These similarities can be traced all the way back to early fish, which have five main bones in their forward fins. Charles Darwin saw all these similarities, which only increased between species that appeared to be closely related, as evidence not of “creation” but of common ancestry. For example, take a look at this elephant skeleton - the feet bones are incredibly similar to other animals with complex feet even though the elephant’s foot is large and flat on the bottom And in whale skeletons, you see what appear to be rear leg bones floating apart from the rest of the skeleton, even though they have no function In modern evolutionary theory, what they now look at is how similar the DNA of different species is. However, even when species are separated by a common ancestor that lived billions of years ago, like humans and oak trees, you still find similarities, like the gene for creating energy in the absence of oxygen. And the X and Y chromosomes of mice and humans are pretty much identical. None of this points to each species being created independently. It points to everything having a common ancestor at some point, sometimes very recently (about 15 million years with people and chimps) but sometimes way back in the past. But its always there.

Question: What was the 70s sitcom “Good Times” about?
Answer: It was largely about the struggles of an African-American family of five living in a two-bedroom apartment in the Chicago projects. James, the patriarch, is hard working, but frequently unemployed due to the economic problems of the era, as is his wife Florida, who has previously worked as a maid for the Findlay household in suburban New York City. Their children are the budding artist James, Jr. (J.J.), the straight-A student Michael, and their daughter Thelma, who hopes to become a fashion designer. James and Florida are constantly trying to keep their kids on the straight and narrow, which is difficult because they too face temptation and find it hard to set a good example. Once, James stumbles on a bag of money and returns most of it, but keeps some when the reward is a grocery voucher. J.J., the eldest, is recruited to a gang, but resists. So is Michael, and he at first gives in. Pitfalls are everywhere, and navigating them is difficult. On his birthday, J.J. is expecting art supplies, but gets a sweater and storms out of the apartment. While he’s out, he’s arrested, but it turns out he’s a victim of mistaken identity - for someone who doesn’t resemble him at all. J.J. falls in love and wants to marry his girlfriend, but when he’s denied permission (at 18, he’s too young under Illinois law) he and his girlfriend go to nearby Indiana only to find out there’s a waiting period. In the meantime, J.J. learns his girlfriend is a junkie, and she dumps him to get a fix. The family grows by one when they save a neighbour who is the subject of abuse, and save her again when her mother comes back only to threaten to beat her. But tragedy strikes as James finds a good job in Mississippi, only to die on the car trip back. So, think “The Honeymooners”, only with more emphasis on real life problems rather than get-rich-quick schemes that go bad.

Question: Why did Terry Fox run across Canada?
Answer: One thing that seems to have been missed in all the other answers was that before his cancer diagnosis and subsequent amputation of his leg, Fox was a pretty good high school athlete. He had wanted to be a basketball player, but was short so took up cross-country running to keep in shape. He eventually made the basketball team and in his final year he was voted his school’s athlete of the year. He planned to go to university to study kinesiology with a goal of becoming a physical education teacher. Some of that was derailed when he found that the knee he thought he had hurt in a minor traffic accident turned out to be an osteosarcoma. That resulted in his leg being amputated. But that didn’t slow him down. He was fitted with an artificial leg and was back running. Then he met Rick Hansen (later “The Man in Motion”) and was recruited to join a wheelchair basketball team. His team won three national championships and he was chosen as an all-star. But it all changed after he learned about Dick Traum, the first amputee to complete the New York City Marathon. Fox decided to follow in his footsteps (literally) and put his cross-country training back into motion so that he could complete a marathon too. But inside, he was seething. Although he had survived cancer, many of his fellow patients did not, and he found that even though his chances were 50% when treated, only a few years earlier they would have been as low as 15%. He secretly formed a goal of running across the country to raise awareness for the need for funding cancer research. After he finished dead last in a 17km road race (which was greeted with massive cheers from the spectators and other participants), he revealed his plans. His mother tried to talk him out of it, but he persevered and the rest, as they say, is history. He was hoping he would maybe raise $1 million. Instead, he raised $1.7 million by the time he had to cut his run short in Ontario.

Question: Why do cops hate it when you “lawyer up”?
Answer: For the same reason you hate it when you’re ready to go on your donut break and someone comes in to order a burger, fries and a coke. Instead of taking it easy, you have to actually do your job for a change. Gathering evidence, talking to witnesses, consulting the district attorney’s office, filling out forms, that sort of thing. Instead, why not just spend 20 minutes convincing someone that it’s in their best interest to talk to you, when it isn’t, then only listening to the stuff that supports your theory rather than to the whole story. Did you know a third of the people who the Innocence Project eventually freed actually confessed to the crime? Bet you didn’t. Let’s get this straight. If you’re under arrest there is nothing, nothing you can do to satisfy the cops of your innocence. Particularly if you are actually innocent. If you’re actually guilty, it actually helps because they will listen to you pin the crime on someone else. Honestly, that happened in Canada where the trial judge actually said the main witness’s description of details at the crime scene proved he was telling the truth that someone else did it. Hell, one guy on death row in the states actually confessed to over 300 murders before someone caught on that he was making it all up to keep himself alive. He was interviewed later and said it was painfully easy - all he had to do was keep trying details until he got the ones that fit, and then blame memory lapses on the number of murders he committed. Think about it - over 300 killers got away because some nutbar claimed their crime and the police couldn’t be bothered to check. That’s why in civilized places like the UK, they assign an entire squad led by a detective inspector to a murder investigation. In the United States, they assign two detectives. Guess who has the higher clearance rate.

Question: What led to northern Canada becoming its own territories instead of being part of the provinces like Quebec or Ontario?
Answer: Oh, that’s complicated. “The Territories” used to be massive. It was pretty much the entire 1670 land grant to the Hudson’s Bay Company, which included the entire watershed of all rivers that emptied into Hudson’s Bay. That even included a bit of what’s now in the United States (it was traded for a bit of the Mississippi watershed in Canada). So let’s take a look at it. In addition, “The Bay” also merged with the North West Company, which pretty much got a grant of all the land where rivers emptied into the Arctic Ocean. In 1870 when the UK transferred all of it’s interest in the land to the new self-governing Dominion of Canada, it was almost entirely inhabited by Hudson Bay company employees, First Nations, Metis and Inuit. That was about to change rapidly. But here’s what the provinces looked like in 1869. Now, the Quebec-Labrador border hadn’t actually been set by this time (it was functionally the northeast coast along the Atlantic) but all this new land being added to the country after Canada bought out “The Bay’s” interest started provincial politicians in Ontario and Quebec rubbing their greedy little hands in delight. There were just a couple of hundred technical issues to sort out, the primary one of which was that although Canada owned what belonged to “The Bay”, the First Nations and Inuit in those territories were likely to fight over their rights to the land the same way that American Indians had done. The first fly in the ointment was the “Red River” or “Selkirk” settlement. A fellow named Selkirk got a land grant from The Bay to attempt to settle an area around Fort Garry, near a key junction of rivers, to keep Americans from claiming the territory of their own. However, the legality of the settlement was not clear and by 1870 most of the inhabitants were Metis - mixed European and Native peoples who were mostly French speaking Catholics. When the Canadian government surveyors showed up there was a massive misunderstanding about land ownership rights that led to a rebellion. The rebels declared a provisional government and had the law on their side. Eventually, Canada conceded and recognized “Manitoba” as a new province. Anyway, over the next fifty years, the Canadian government worked with the local First Nations populations on treaties (the “numbered treaties”) and despite a rebellion in 1885 (that was led by the same guy in charge of the 1870 rebellion, Louis Riel) settlement of the west was mostly peaceful. Over time the North-West Territory was split up into new provinces with bits going to Quebec and Ontario, more being added to Manitoba, and much of the rest going to the new provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan in 1905. More land was added to Manitoba and Ontario later after Treaty 9. Logistically, this was all making sense because really the only way that Canada could control all this territory was through its railway, which was completed from Ontario to British Columbia in 1885. A second railway was built by the early 20th century, but it wasn’t as lucrative and the Canadian government took it over in the 1960s, calling it “Canadian National Railways”. Yukon Territory was formed in 1896 in response to a flood of Americans crossing the border looking for gold in the Klondike so that the North-West Mounted Police had jurisdiction over the area. Right now, we have three territories. Yukon, which was the part of the North-West Company territory west of the Rocky Mountains that did not clearly pass to The Bay when the two companies merged. Most of it is unceded territory. Nunavut, which is recognized as being unceded Inuit territory. Some Inuit have ceded territory to Canada and that’s the yellow islands at top left. The Northwest Territories, which are mostly ceded First Nations land, but a small part of it remained unceded.
